lead: An LR parser reads tokens from left to right and builds a rightmost derivation in reverse. To do this it must remember which production is being recognised and how much of that production is already on its stack. An LR(0) item stores exactly that: a production with a dot showing the current position. Closure and goto turn a grammar into a finite automaton of item sets. The parser uses this automaton as a table. Parser generators such as YACC build such tables from a grammar, so the same idea powers real compilers.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for shift-reduce parsing and handles, and Unit 2 for context-free grammars, derivations and parse trees.

blocks.text: An LR(0) item is a production with a dot (.) in its right side: A → α . β. A is a nonterminal; α and β are strings of grammar symbols. The dot separates symbols already matched (α) from symbols still expected (β). If the dot is at the end, A → α ., the production is complete and can be reduced. A dot before a terminal calls for a shift. A dot before a nonterminal may start that nonterminal's productions.

Closure completes an item set. For a set I, closure(I) is the smallest set containing I and following this rule: if A → α . B β is in the set and B → γ is a production, add B → . γ. Repeat until no new item appears. The dot does not move.

Add the augmented production S' → S. S' is a new start nonterminal; S is the original start symbol. For S → C C, C → c C | d, start from S' → . S. Closure adds S → . C C, then C → . c C and C → . d. This is state I0.

Goto(I, X) moves the dot past one symbol X. Take every item in I with X just after the dot, make a new item with the dot after X, then take closure: goto(I, X) = closure({ A → α X . β | A → α . X β ∈ I }). If no item has X after the dot, goto is empty. Closure adds items; goto moves the dot one place.

Build the canonical collection this way. Start with I0 = closure({S' → . S}). For every state and grammar symbol X, compute goto(I, X). If the result is nonempty and new, make it a new state. Repeat. Finitely many items means this stops.

For the example, the states are I0 to I6. I0 is S' → . S, S → . C C, C → . c C, C → . d. I1 is S' → S .. I2 is S → C . C, C → . c C, C → . d. I3 is C → c . C, C → . c C, C → . d. I4 is C → d .. I5 is S → C C .. I6 is C → c C .. The figure shows the transitions.

ACTION maps state and terminal to shift, reduce, accept or error. GOTO maps state and nonterminal to a state. Suppose state i has a shift item A → α . a β for terminal a, and goto(Ii, a) = Ij. Then ACTION[i, a] = shift j, written s j. The parser pushes a and state j. If state i has a complete item A → α . with A ≠ S', then ACTION[i, a] = reduce A → α, written r j, for every terminal a and for $. LR(0) ignores the next token in a reduce. If the item is S' → S ., ACTION[i, $] = accept. Blank means error. For nonterminal A, GOTO[i, A] = j when goto(Ii, A) = Ij.

LR(0) tables can conflict. A shift/reduce conflict means one cell wants shift and reduce; it happens when a state has a complete item and a shift item on the same terminal. A reduce/reduce conflict means two complete items give two reductions for the same terminal. The example has no conflicts: states I0, I2, I3 shift; I4 reduces C → d; I5 reduces S → C C; I6 reduces C → c C; I1 accepts.

figure.caption: Closure of S′ → .S gives I0, and goto on S, C, c and d reaches the other six item sets. The green states hold one finished item each, so they reduce on every symbol without a conflict.

spec.aria: Seven LR(0) item sets I0 to I6 joined by goto arrows labelled S, C, c and d, with I1 the accept state and I4, I5 and I6 the reduce states.

examples.question: For the grammar S → C C, C → c C | d with augmented production S' → S, compute closure(I0), all goto sets, the canonical LR(0) collection, and the ACTION/GOTO table. State whether the grammar is LR(0).
steps: Number productions: 0 S'→S; 1 S→CC; 2 C→cC; 3 C→d. Terminals c,d; $ ends input.
Goto sets: goto(I0,S)=I1; goto(I0,C)=I2; goto(I0,c)=I3; goto(I0,d)=I4; goto(I2,C)=I5; goto(I2,c)=I3; goto(I2,d)=I4; goto(I3,C)=I6; goto(I3,c)=I3; goto(I3,d)=I4. Others empty.
Item sets: I1={S'→S.}; I2={S→C.C,C→.cC,C→.d}; I3={C→c.C,C→.cC,C→.d}; I4={C→d.}; I5={S→CC.}; I6={C→cC.}.
ACTION: I0 c=s3,d=s4; I1 $=acc; I2 c=s3,d=s4; I3 c=s3,d=s4; I4 c,d,$=r3; I5 c,d,$=r1; I6 c,d,$=r2. Blank is error.
GOTO: I0 S=1,C=2; I2 C=5; I3 C=6.
Summary: 7 states; 6 shift entries, 9 reduce entries, 1 accept entry, 4 goto entries, 0 conflicts. No state has a complete item plus a terminal shift, and none has two complete items.
examples.answer: The automaton has 7 states; the ACTION/GOTO table has 6 shift entries, 9 reduce entries, 1 accept entry, 4 goto entries and 0 conflicts, so the grammar is LR(0).

traps: Closure adds items; it never moves the dot. Goto moves the dot past exactly one symbol and then closes. If you close after moving several symbols, the states are wrong.
A dot before a nonterminal starts closure. A dot before a terminal causes a shift; it does not add productions.
In LR(0), a reduce item is reduced for every terminal and $, not only for FOLLOW(A). That is why LR(0) tables conflict; SLR fixes this in Chapter 3.3.
The completed item S' → S . gives accept on $, not a reduce action. Never reduce by the augmented start production.
GOTO columns exist only for nonterminals; ACTION columns only for terminals. A shift entry is s j, a reduce entry is r j; blank means error, not state 0.

quiz.q: Define an LR(0) item. What does the dot mean?
quiz.a: A production with a dot in its right side. Symbols left of the dot are matched; symbols right of the dot are expected.

quiz.q: Why does closure add items with the dot at the start of a production?
quiz.a: When the dot is before nonterminal B, the parser may next start any B production. Closure adds B→.γ so the state lists all possibilities. It does not move the dot.

quiz.q: For I0={S'→.S, S→.CC, C→.cC, C→.d}, compute goto(I0,c).
quiz.a: Move the dot past c: C→c.C. Closure adds C→.cC and C→.d. Result {C→c.C, C→.cC, C→.d}=I3.

quiz.q: In the example table, what is ACTION[4,c], ACTION[4,d], ACTION[4,$]?
quiz.a: All are r3, reduce by C→d.

quiz.q: Explain how a shift/reduce conflict arises in an LR(0) state.
quiz.a: The state has a complete item A→α. and a shift item B→β.aγ. The complete item asks reduce on every terminal including a; the shift item asks shift a. The same ACTION cell gets two actions.

quiz.q: The example grammar is LR(0). Justify from its item sets.
quiz.a: No state has a complete item with a terminal shift, and no state has two complete items. Thus there is no shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict; the table is deterministic.

quiz.q: State the difference between closure and goto in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Closure adds dot-at-start items for a nonterminal after the dot. Goto moves the dot past one grammar symbol and then takes closure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as YACC and Bison build LR automata and report conflicts in terms of item sets. Modern compiler courses often connect these item sets to parser combinators and error messages. Search for “canonical LR(0) collection”, “item set closure”, and “shift/reduce conflict example”.
